name: Hana Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Emre and I farm the hill farm my father farmed, up at the end of Quarry Road. Three hundred ewes, a few house cows for milk, oats and potatoes on the flat bit, and hay for winter. We took a mortgage on the farmhouse to buy out my brother's share when Dad died, so every lamb we sell is really going to the bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five, check the ewes on foot because the quad doesn't like the steep bit, milk the cows by hand because there's only three of them, then breakfast for Elif and Yusuf before the school bus. The rest is fences, feeding, the potatoes, whatever the season says. I don't have one of those smartphones, and Emre only uses his to ring the vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Farming is weather, animals and hard work, and a computer can't do any of that. People in the city get excited about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for us. We'd carry on as we have since my grandfather's time. The worry would be the same as always: the lamb price and the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Lambing in April, shearing in June, hay in July, sell the lambs in September. If there's any spare money I'd put it into the mortgage, not into gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how life should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bank is always the worry. How close to the edge are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One bad winter. If we lose forty ewes in the snow like in my father's last year, we'd be asking my brother-in-law for a loan. We've done it once and I'd rather not again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone in the family use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elif, my daughter, she does her homework with something on the school laptop. I told her to do it with her own head. She rolled her eyes at me, like they do at thirteen.

S0.say: She wouldn't be surprised, because farming is weather, animals and hard work that computers can't do. People in the city get excited about everything.
S0.think: It means nothing for her family, who would carry on as they have since her grandfather's time. The worries stay the same: lamb prices and the bank.
S0.do: Keeps the usual year of lambing, shearing, hay and lamb sales. Puts any spare money into the mortgage rather than new tools.
S0.feel: Calm, as she thinks life should be.
S0.quote: I told her to do it with her own head.
S0.fieldNote: She sees AI as a city fashion with no place on a hill farm. Her real fear is a hard winter like the one in her father's last year, and needing to borrow from family again. Her daughter's use of AI for homework is a small source of friction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines are for the big flat farms, not for hills like ours. Let them have their robots. People will always want lamb raised properly, by a family that knows the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a little that the lamb price falls if the big farms get cheaper. But the hill is the hill, a robot would fall off it. I think we'd be all right, just poorer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are, and wait to see what happens to prices. I wouldn't buy anything. If the lamb price dropped, I'd sell more direct to people at the mosque and in town, the way my mother used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Like hearing thunder from the next valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot would fall off your hill. Are you sure about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. Emre showed me a video once of a robot dog walking up stairs. I told him to turn it off. But I'd want to see it on a wet hill in February before I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help farmers like you through this, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own families first, and the community. I don't want government money with a hundred forms attached. Give us a fair price for lamb and we'll look after ourselves.

S1.say: Machines belong on big flat farms, not hills like hers, and people will always want lamb raised properly by a family. Let the big farms have their robots.
S1.think: She worries a little that lamb prices fall if big farms get cheaper. But she believes robots can't manage the hill, so the family would be all right, just poorer.
S1.do: Carries on as normal and watches lamb prices without buying any new equipment. Sells more lamb directly to people at the mosque and in town if prices fall, as her mother did.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, like thunder from the next valley.
S1.quote: But I'd want to see it on a wet hill in February before I believe it.
S1.fieldNote: Her confidence rests on the steep land, but she admits she isn't sure when pushed. She wants a fair price rather than government help, which fits her outlook. Direct selling to her community is her fallback, a habit from her mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast, and nobody asked people like us. Big companies decided and the rest of us have to live with it. I'd say families and communities will have to hold together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years and everything changes. If the big farms can make lamb for half the price, nobody buys mine, even at the mosque, because everybody's money gets tight. The bank doesn't care that my grandfather built the barn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut to the bone: no new clothes, no trip to my sister's at the end of Ramadan. Emre would look for any work going in town, though there wouldn't be much. And I'd talk to my brother and my brother-in-law about whether the family could help with the mortgage for a year, which would hurt my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake listening to the wind and doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elif and Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're a family and we'll manage, and that they need to work hard at school. I'd tell Elif maybe her computer homework isn't so silly after all. She'd love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider any government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was that or losing the farm, yes, I'd take it, and I'd hate it. But I'd go to family first. That's how we were raised.

S2.say: This is going too fast and nobody asked people like her; big companies decided for everyone. Families and communities will have to hold together.
S2.think: In two years big farms could make lamb at half the price, and even her community buyers would have less money. The bank wouldn't care about her family's history on the land.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone, including the family trip at the end of Ramadan, while Emre looks for work in town. Asks her brother and brother-in-law to help with the mortgage for a year, despite her pride.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums while listening to the wind.
S2.quote: The bank doesn't care that my grandfather built the barn.
S2.fieldNote: Her sense of family history runs straight into the reality of the mortgage. She turns to family before government, and accepts state help only as a last resort. She softens on her daughter's AI homework, a small sign she knows the world has moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to prepare their own way, without the government telling them what to do. Families should be getting their children into good trades now. That's what I'd say at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps me get the mortgage down a bit and get Elif through school. But I still don't want robots on my hill. I think we'd hold on longer than people expect, just with less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare bit into the mortgage. I'd build up the direct lamb sales so we have our own customers, not just the auction. And I'd tell Elif to pick a good trade or profession, maybe pharmacy, something people always need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than the slow one, less than the fast one. I'd be watching the lamb price every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about using any new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my neighbour Ali bought one and it worked for three winters. He's sensible, not a show-off. But even then I'd want to see it with my own eyes on his land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold on longer than people expect. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we don't need much. We grow our own potatoes, we have milk, we have meat. City people would panic before we did.

S3.say: Five years gives families enough time to prepare their own way without the government telling them what to do. Families should be getting children into good trades now.
S3.think: Five years helps her pay down some of the mortgage and see her daughter through school. She still wouldn't want robots on her hill and expects to hold on longer than people think, with less money.
S3.do: Puts every spare bit of money into the mortgage and builds up direct lamb sales so the family has its own customers. Encourages her daughter towards a steady profession like pharmacy.
S3.feel: Anxious, in between the slow and fast scenarios, and checking the lamb price weekly.
S3.quote: City people would panic before we did.
S3.fieldNote: Self-sufficiency is her anchor: potatoes, milk and meat at home. She would only consider new machines after a trusted neighbour proved them over three winters. Extra time goes into paying debt and the children's futures, not changing how she farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so people should stop complaining and get on with it. Teach your children a trade, keep your family close, work hard. That's what's always worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, in ten years I'd be fifty-three and the children would have left home. I think the farm would still be ours, but smaller, maybe just sheep, and we'd live more simply. That's not the worst thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd pay the mortgage down and keep the direct sales going. I'd make sure Elif and Yusuf both have a skill that isn't the farm. And Emre and I would talk about what we can keep going ourselves if the farm stops paying, the house, the garden, the animals for our own table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's further off. I'd think about it on the bad days, not every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the farm stops paying, would you consider selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. My father would turn in his grave. We'd keep it even if it was just a big garden with a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this future that you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a machine took the worst of the winter feeding, carrying bales up the hill in the snow, I wouldn't cry. But I'd still be out there checking the sheep myself.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so people should stop complaining and get on with it. Teach children a trade, keep families close and work hard, as has always worked.
S4.think: In ten years she'd be 53 with the children grown, and the farm would probably still be theirs but smaller and simpler. She doesn't see that as the worst outcome.
S4.do: Keeps paying down the mortgage and growing direct sales, and makes sure both children have skills outside farming. Plans with Emre what they could keep going for themselves if the farm stops paying.
S4.feel: Anxious, but only on the bad days because it feels further off.
S4.quote: We'd keep it even if it was just a big garden with a view.
S4.fieldNote: Holding on to the land matters more to her than making a living from it. She refuses to consider selling but quietly admits she'd welcome a machine for the worst winter work. Her answer to the long timeline is about family, not technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. There'd be no time for anything, and the bank would come before the family could help. What would help is a fair price for lamb, and maybe the bank giving farmers a year's break on the mortgage instead of a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things are hard we go to the mosque and people help each other, with food, with work, with a loan without interest. Whatever happens with these machines, that doesn't change.

headlineQuote: Give us a fair price for lamb and we'll look after ourselves.
portrait: Hana Yilmaz is 43 and farms her late father's hill farm on Quarry Road with her husband Emre, keeping sheep, a few house cows and some oats and potatoes, with a mortgage taken out to buy out her brother. She is traditional, values family and faith, distrusts government handouts, and does not own a smartphone. She is calm or only uneasy in the milder scenarios, trusting that robots can't manage her steep land. AGI in two years leaves her alarmed and leaning on family for the mortgage, while with five or ten years she pays down debt, builds direct sales and steers her children towards other trades. She would never sell the land.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time and the bank would come before the family could help.
whatWouldHelp: A fair price for lamb, and banks giving farmers a year's break on the mortgage rather than a handout.
